item.title: After Black October, OffSec Turns PHPH2Shell and Other New Vulnerabilities Into Hands-On Labs
item.description:
OffSec built 14 labs on real CVEs in two weeks. Its Level 20 offer takes $550 off Learn One for learners ready to train against threats like these.

OffSec, the world’s leading provider of hands-on cybersecurity training and certifications, released more than 80 hands-on labs in the last two weeks of October as Black October crippled government and university websites across Europe. The labs give security teams a safe place to attack and defend the same kinds of flaws making headlines. Fourteen are built on real CVEs disclosed this year. They include a free lab on PHP2Shell, the PHP flaw at the center of the month’s disclosure wave.

Black October is the name the security community gave to a cluster of critical disclosures in late October. At its center was PHP2Shell (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619). The flaws let attackers run code on web servers without logging in. Researchers at Calif and Wiz found the flaws with help from AI models. Amazon spotted an exploitation attempt on Oct. 17, four days before public disclosure. CERT-EU told organizations that could not patch right away to isolate internet-facing apps from public networks. CISA urged immediate patching. The same day GitLab patched a maximum-severity flaw that let unauthenticated users run code on its servers. CrowdStrike reported four threat actors running campaigns in which AI agents make decisions and execute commands.

The pace reflects a larger shift. AI now helps find flaws and turn them into working exploits. An AI agent can compare a vulnerable release against its patched version and see exactly what changed. That shrinks the window defenders have to understand a flaw and act on it.

“AI has lowered the skill ceiling for attackers,” said Alex “Sickness” Uifalvi, Security Researcher and architect at OffSec. “Going from a patch to a working exploit used to take a skilled team up to a week. An agent can cut that by a big chunk. Defenders need to get their hands on these flaws while they are still in the news. That is why our team builds labs on real CVEs as fast as we can. You learn what an attack looks like by running it and stopping it yourself.”

OffSec’s new labs, listed in its Oct. 19–25 and Oct. 26–Nov. 2 weekly updates, cover both sides of an incident, and include:

  • Offensive Labs built on recent CVEs in Kestra, Hermes WebUI, WordPress 7.0.2, the Algernon web server and a chained Vite and Uptime Kuma exposure.
  • Defensive Labs where learners secure vulnerable versions of Spring, Kestra and Next.js.
  • Incident Investigations modeled on real attack types. These include ransomware that began with a help desk call, an email compromise that rerouted a client payment, a breached SSL VPN appliance and an intrusion at a hydroelectric plant.
  • AI Targets such as an AI-driven tool marketplace with an automated reviewer and agent.

OffSec CEO Ning Wang said fast-moving flaws like PHP2Shell are now the norm.

“These vulnerabilities are being found by AI agents and that will happen more and more,” said CEO Wang. “You need to very quickly understand how a flaw works and how to defend against it. When PHP2Shell hit, we acted instantly to develop a new lab and a blog to begin teaching people how the attack works and how to stop it. Every organization that cares about its business risk needs to be on top of these things. Your red team and your blue team both need to know how to use AI to do their jobs. It’s no longer a nice-to-do. It’s a must-do.”

Level 20: Same Game, New Level

OffSec is marking 20 years of hands-on training with Level 20, a year-end offer for individual learners. Learn One is $550 off through Jan. 4, 2027. Security professionals who want to learn AI red teaming can now train for OSAI (OffSec AI Red Teamer) through Learn One. This is the first time OSAI is part of a Learn One offer. Its AI-300 course covers attacks on AI models, large language models and autonomous agents.

A Learn One Subscription Includes:

  • One 200- or 300-level OffSec course such as PEN-200 for the OSCP penetration testing certification or AI-300 for OSAI
  • 365 days of course and lab access
  • Two attempts at the certification exam
  • More than 200 Proving Grounds Practice labs
  • Bonus KLCP and OSWP courses and exams

The PHP2Shell lab is free to use on Proving Grounds Play. Claim the Level 20 offer at learn.offsec.com/level-20-promo.

About OffSec

OffSec (formerly Offensive Security) is the world’s leading provider of high-fidelity cybersecurity training and certifications. Built on a foundation of excellence, integrity, and the relentless “Try Harder” ethos, OffSec empowers individuals and organizations to outsmart evolving cyber threats through rigorous, hands-on learning.

From its beginnings to today, OffSec has set the elite standard for cybersecurity proficiency, earning global recognition and the implicit trust of the world’s most elite security teams. With a comprehensive ecosystem ranging from the industry-defining OSCP to the cutting-edge OSAI (OffSec AI Red Teamer), OffSec is the definitive benchmark for validating real-world technical skills in an increasingly automated world.

item.title: Optimizely confirms massive cyberattack on customer websites injected stealer malware
item.description:
Attackers apparently from China used an authentication security hole within the popular Optimizely AI platform for marketers to steal from at least 178 sites owned by some of the planet’s largest companies. 

Named victims featured vendors including Zoom, Paychex, Equifax, and GitLab, and end-user enterprises including Starbucks, IKEA, Mattel, American Eagle, Air France, Mutual of Omaha, Heineken, Home Chef, Cinnabon, American Eagle, Levi, Costco and HSBC.

Salesforce issued a statement confirming that it had also been impacted by the attack.

“Salesforce is investigating unauthorized modifications to scripts provided by Optimizely and used on certain Salesforce websites,” it wrote in an email statement. “As a precaution, Salesforce is confirming that Optimizely scripts are disabled across preview and production instances.”

The attacks were discovered by UK-based security researcher Scott Helme, the founder of Report URI, who said in an interview that his team had confirmed 178 victims, but that there could be more. “That’s the number that we directly observed and that all carried the same infection,” he said. 

Helme published a report about the attacks on Monday, in which he described an attack methodology where an Optimizely capability in its Web Experimentation product facilitating adding members to a site’s development team was leveraged to insert malware into the sites.

“The malware was a multi-purpose kit. It swapped cryptocurrency wallet addresses for the attacker’s, skimmed payment cards, stole cookies and screenshots, and on iPhones and iPads it delivered the Coruna and DarkSword iOS exploit kits,” Helme wrote. “The important lesson here is that trusted JavaScript doesn’t always remain trustworthy. A website can be compromised through a third-party dependency without its own code or infrastructure ever being breached.” 

Optimizely customers load a JavaScript “snippet” from Optimizely’s CDN onto their sites which contains Optimizely code, the customer’s A/B tests, and an optional field called Project JavaScript containing custom code written by the customer. The report said that attackers inserted their own code into the customer’s Project JavaScript and left the rest of each snippet untouched. “The file was still served from cdn[.]Optimizely[.]com, with Optimizely’s certificate, from a host that every affected site already trusted,” it noted.

The report described how the observed attack worked. “The script watches form submissions and every fetch/XHR POST for a card number, expiry date and CVV,” it said. “When it has all three, it sends them to https://1688360[.]cc/card[.]php with navigator.sendBeacon. Cards entered in hosted payment iframes [such as] Stripe, Adyen and similar were out of its reach. Cards typed into a site’s own form fields were not.”

Analyst questions the claims of a fix

Optimizely, which did not reply to an interview request, confirmed the attacks on its site. In an email shared with customers, Optimizely said that attackers “exploited a vulnerability in the Experimentation account signup flow. They used it to impersonate a user and add malicious JavaScript to some customer projects. We have blocked access to the vulnerable path and deployed a fix.”

The email also said that the company had “ended active sessions and revoked tokens and reset access for affected user accounts” and that it also had “removed the injected code from affected projects” and “blocked any code from being delivered in Cloudflare.”

The company used highly confident wording to describe its fix, saying that “the Optimizely Experimentation platform is fully secured” and that “modification of Javascript no longer possible.”

Frank Dickson, principal analyst at Dickson Research, raised an eyebrow at those claims.

To begin with, he noted a discrepancy in the timelines published by the vendor and the security researcher. “Optimizely puts the first malicious write at 07:51. Report URI saw the BBC’s Optimizely snippet loading attacker code at 04:21, three and a half hours earlier,” he said. “The forensics report should reconcile that gap. Customers need the real start time to scope their exposure.”

As well, he pointed out, “Optimizely seems very comfortable stating absolutes early in a forensics investigation. Those are verdicts from a company whose forensics are still underway and whose timeline disagrees with outside research.”

No responsibility for the attack claimed

Helme speculated in an interview that the attackers were a small group of thieves, almost certainly coming from China, noting that he saw extensive Chinese writing in the code and that the attacks “tie back to infrastructure that has been used by other Chinese actors.”

“They are either Chinese or they really want us to think that they are Chinese,” Helme said, adding that the nature of what was stolen makes it highly unlikely the attackers were state actors. State actors, he said, would likely have used the malware on major news sites to create and spread false stories. 

Asked if his team could verify Optimizely’s claim that it had fixed the hole, he said that he couldn’t yet. Some of the infected sites were cleaned up, but he has to wait to see if they get reinfected before concluding that the original hole had been closed. 

Recommendation to customers ‘concerning’

Dickson said that one line in Optimizely’s email to customers was especially concerning.

“Optimizely’s documentation tells customers to allow ‘unsafe-eval‘ in their policy. At HSBC, the policy blocked the main payload and the data theft, but a backup copy of the malicious code ran anyway through that setting. A vendor’s setup guide should not quietly loosen its customers’ defenses,” Dickson said. “Restrict script-src to the hosts a page actually needs. Lock down connect-src so stolen data has nowhere to go. Drop ‘unsafe-eval‘ wherever possible. Start in report-only mode so nothing breaks.”

He added, “the Optimizely attack may be about as bad as a third-party script compromise gets. Optimizely owes its customers a clear explanation of how one flaw reached so many unrelated companies.”

This article originally appeared on CSOonline.

item.title: Can your business withstand a destructive cyberattack?
item.description:
Nearly every cyber recovery plan relies on assumptions about how recovery will unfold. Teams expect incidents can be fully contained before recovery begins, that recovery can proceed in a mostly linear sequence, and that they will have sufficient visibility into system and data dependencies.

Destructive cyberattacks can quickly challenge those assumptions. The 2026 Cohesity Global Cyber Resilience Report found that among organizations that experienced a material cyberattack in the previous 12 months, 70% saw the scope of affected systems expand beyond the initial assessment, 61% identified moderate or significant gaps in how their plans accounted for dependencies, and 76% exceeded their recovery time objectives, with recovery taking nearly twice as long as planned.

The findings also point to a broader gap in how organizations approach recovery. For 78% of organizations, cyber response and recovery plans focus more on restoring systems than on maintaining critical operations and serving customers during recovery. That imbalance matters when the damage extends further than anticipated or when getting everything back takes longer than planned.

Organizations need a clear understanding of what must remain operational in the meantime. One approach is to define a Minimum Viable Company (MVC), the smallest version of the organization that can continue serving customers and maintaining critical operations during a disruption. Establishing an MVC requires identifying essential business services and the data, applications, identities, infrastructure, and third-party dependencies needed to support them. Yet only 22% of organizations have formally documented and tested an MVC.

AI is adding another layer of complexity to cyber resilience planning and is already widespread, with 99% of organizations reporting use of AI systems, applications, workflows, or machine learning models. Even so, only 39% say their response and recovery plans comprehensively account for cyberattacks targeting AI. Almost every organization surveyed also expects its plan will need to change to address emerging threats from frontier AI capabilities. Just 3% say their current plan is equipped for those conditions.

No plan can predict exactly how a destructive cyberattack will unfold. CIOs can, however, pressure-test what happens when key expectations break down. What if more systems are affected than anticipated? What if recovery takes twice as long? What if restored data can’t immediately be trusted or users lose access to essential systems? The value of that preparation is clear among organizations that have done the MVC work: 92% of those with a documented and tested MVC say it informed or influenced their recovery priorities.

Testing scenarios like these can expose weaknesses before a crisis does. It can also help organizations make the decisions that matter most during a disruption: which operations need to continue, what they depend on, and how they can be sustained until full recovery is complete.

item.title: Drive revenue visibility, operational control, and competitive edge with CPQ
item.description:
Reducing the time it takes to generate quotes and recognize revenue is crucial for every business. Not only does it create stable cash flow, quick and accurate information improves the customer experience – leading to more repeat business.

However, when transactions include large product catalogues, complex offerings and customizable solutions, this creates a challenge for sales teams turning quotes to cash. Added to this is a dynamic macroeconomic climate, with tariffs and supply chain disruptions creating an extra layer of complexity. This is where configure, price, quote (CPQ) software comes into play, as it automates product configuration, pricing, and quote generation for sales teams.

“The speed in selling is so critical and important. Sometimes you’re having conversations with the customers, and you want to be able to simply produce a quote and show them this is how your configuration looks like. If you’re not able to do that, you lose that momentum while selling,” says Srikanth Akkiraju, Chief Transformation Officer at Service Now, speaking to enterprise CIOs about the topic in a recent webcast [insert link to webcast].

To help companies stay agile and keep pace with multiple demands, ServiceNow CPQ uses embedded AI to manage and maintain the thousands of rules and configurations. In fact, Akkiraju notes the company’s agentic AI capabilities were recognized in The Forrester Wave™: Configure, Price, Quote Solutions, Q4 2026, which named ServiceNow a Leader and a Customer Favorite.

He also cites a number of customers who’ve seen tangible results using ServiceNow CPQ. Global golf cart manufacturer Club Car replaced its legacy systems with one configuration engine. This led to 2,000 qualified leads per month generated online, a 17% consumer conversion rate and five-times faster dealer reorders. “That’s a huge new revenue generation channel.” Manufacturing business Keysight Technologies had a similar experience. By moving to ServiceNow CPQ, it decreased quote processing time by 40% and reduced configuration setup and maintenance time by 50 to 80%. Akkiraju points to the impact on sales velocity and capacity: “That’s a huge win in efficiency, but if you are 40% faster, you can do more quotes and be in front of the customer [more]. So, you’re also getting more opportunities in.”

Several European airport operations companies have achieved similar results – not just for CPQ but the whole end-to-end business process. “They’re using it for the whole lead to cash process and service. So that way they also connect the dots across the full value chain, which means the whole value chain is moving 20 to 40% faster.”

To maximize value through CPQ, Akkiraju advises the software is not used in isolation from the full value chain. “So, you’re not just doing an individual quote or a point in time quote. You really want the customer to have the best configuration, and to deliver it on time and in budget, and make sure you can service these configurations,” he says. “Value can be derived better when you connect the dots end to end and use CPQ to become the spider in the web to enable the whole process to be seamless in for the customer.”

To learn more on how to unlock competitive advantage with AI-powered CPQ, click here to watch the full webinar.

item.title: The AI deregulation illusion: Why CIOs face more rules, not fewer
item.description:
If you follow the headlines coming out of Washington, you might conclude that AI regulation is on its way out. The administration has made reducing regulatory barriers a priority, arguing that lighter oversight is essential to American innovation and competitiveness. But for CIOs responsible for deploying AI across large enterprises, the reality is exactly the opposite.

While Washington pushes for fewer restrictions, states are passing new AI legislation, international regulators are enforcing increasingly complex requirements, and lawmakers are turning their attention to how businesses actually use AI. Essentially, while AI may be getting deregulated at the federal level, it’s becoming more regulated in practice.

For organizations operating across state and national borders, this creates an increasingly difficult challenge. An AI application that meets requirements in one jurisdiction may trigger additional obligations in another. And as AI becomes embedded in more business-critical processes, the consequences of inadequate governance are growing.

As Washington steps back, states step in

Just last year the White House issued an executive order seeking to limit conflicting state AI regulations and establish a more consistent national approach. But an executive order does not automatically invalidate state laws, and states are continuing to legislate.

Consider the wave of AI legislation enacted over the past year:

California’s Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53), effective this January, requires covered frontier AI developers to publish safety frameworks and report critical safety incidents. New York followed with its RAISE Act, establishing similar obligations beginning in January 2027. In September alone, California Gov. Gavin Newsom signed 11 more AI safety bills into law, capping a 2026 legislative year that saw nearly 30 AI-related measures enacted.

Illinois went further in July 2026, enacting the Artificial Intelligence Safety Measures Act (SB 315). Effective January 2027, it requires covered frontier model developers to implement safety frameworks, report serious incidents and, for the largest developers, undergo independent compliance audits.

Perhaps most notable of all is the Texas Responsible Artificial Intelligence Governance Act (TRAIGA), a state law that regulates the development and deployment of AI systems in the state that took effect this year. TRAIGA establishes an intent-based liability model rather than a broad pre-deployment risk assessment requirement.

Other legislation reaches directly into enterprise operations:

In May 2026, Colorado enacted SB 26-189, replacing its earlier AI law with a framework governing automated decision-making technologies used in consequential decisions, including employment, lending and housing. Beginning January 2027, covered businesses will face disclosure and other obligations, while consumers gain rights concerning inaccurate personal data.

Colorado also enacted the Conversational Artificial Intelligence Service Operator Requirements Act (HB 26-1263) in May, introducing requirements for conversational AI services, including disclosures and protections for minors.

For global enterprises, the complexity increases considerably:

The European Union’s AI Act is moving into active enforcement. In July 2026, the EU adopted the AI Omnibus amendments, simplifying certain requirements and extending implementation deadlines for high-risk systems into 2027 and 2028. The underlying framework remains intact, with obligations addressing transparency, prohibited AI practices, general-purpose models and high-risk applications.

Consider a multinational company using AI to screen job applicants, evaluate customer eligibility for financial products, or automate service interactions. The same application could face different requirements depending on where it operates, which individuals it affects and how its outputs influence decisions.

Even within a single organization, the same underlying model might power a low-risk productivity assistant and a highly consequential employment application. The model may be identical, but the risks and regulatory obligations are not. This makes AI governance a different animal compared to traditional software compliance.

The lesson? Organizations can’t just certify a model once and assume every application built on it is compliant everywhere. They must understand how AI is used, what information it accesses, which decisions it influences and which jurisdictional requirements apply.

Governing AI you can’t see

Regulatory fragmentation is exposing a deeper problem. As AI becomes more operational, many enterprises lack comprehensive visibility into their AI systems.

Organizations may have approved several enterprise AI platforms, while individual departments independently integrate models into customer service, analytics, software development and decision-making workflows. Meanwhile, third-party vendors continue embedding AI into existing products, often expanding an organization’s AI footprint without corresponding governance processes.

Agentic AI makes this even more consequential. Systems are increasingly capable of accessing sensitive information, interacting with enterprise applications and taking actions vs. generating responses. When something goes wrong, organizations must be able to determine which system was involved, what data it accessed, how it behaved and which safeguards were in place.

The same goes for shadow AI. We know it’s happening, but as more solutions become available and workarounds are established, the harder it is to govern.

Creating a unified foundation for AI compliance

The natural response to fragmented regulation might be to create separate compliance processes for every jurisdiction. But given 280 laws were passed just this year (with weeks to go), that approach is unsustainable.

Instead, CIOs should establish a common foundation for responsible AI across the enterprise, applying additional safeguards where specific regulations or use cases require them. That starts with maintaining an accurate inventory of AI applications, models, agents and third-party integrations.

It also requires continuous evaluation. Testing an AI application before deployment is necessary, but insufficient. Changes in prompts, data, integrations, or underlying models can introduce new risks after deployment. Organizations need ongoing monitoring for accuracy, reliability, security, privacy, bias and adherence to business policies, with documented evidence of testing and remediation.

Governance must also extend beyond the model. A reliable model can still create serious problems when connected to sensitive databases, external tools, or automated workflows without appropriate access controls. But most importantly, responsible AI can’t be defined as a collection of policy documents. Principles around fairness, transparency and accountability must translate into measurable technical controls and operational processes.

The stakes are rising and becoming more complex

Federal lawmakers may eventually establish a national AI framework that supersedes some state requirements. Courts may also reshape the regulatory landscape. That said, CIOs can’t assume simpler, streamlined rules are coming. Even with a unified federal approach, multinational organizations will face distinct international obligations.

The organizations best prepared for this will be those that understand where their AI operates, understand its risks, continuously evaluate its behavior and can demonstrate appropriate oversight. The takeaway for CIOs is simple: federal deregulation does not equal enterprise deregulation. It means creating the conditions for AI adoption to scale responsibly.

item.title: AI is blurring the lines between CIO, CISO and CRO
item.description:
At 09:24 on a quiet Tuesday, an AI agent spots suspicious privileged activity. It concludes the safest move is to turn off the identity service. So it does.

Everything works as designed. The agent has its own identity. Its credentials are scoped. The action lands in a log nobody can alter. The policy was clear enough: don’t interrupt production services without approval. The agent read the policy, weighed the threat and decided containment counted as approval.

By 09:30, the call centre can’t log in. Neither can the payments team.

Three good executives arrive in the same room with three different instincts. The CIO wants the service back. The CISO wants it kept down until someone proves the threat has gone. The CRO is doing quieter arithmetic, working out how long the firm can limp before it breaches a tolerance the board signed off last spring.

So who decided? And who decides now?

I’ve watched versions of that room more times than I’d like. For years I thought the fix was better people. A few years ago, I realized I had it backwards. The people were fine. The decision had no home. Agents have made that problem faster, and much harder to hide.

Gartner is right, up to a point

Gartner pointed this out in September. Its argument is blunt. Companies are governing autonomous agents with tools built for human decision-makers. As Vice President Analyst George Spafford puts it, “Written corporate policies cannot physically stop an agent from making a destructive error.”

Gartner predicts that by 2029, at least 70% of organizations running agentic AI in production within infrastructure and operations will suffer a material service, security or cost incident. It ties those incidents partly to weak runtime controls. That’s a forecast, and its scope is narrower than the headline suggests. The direction still feels right to me.

The prescription is sensible. Give every agent its own identity and an accountable owner. Grant access for the task, then revoke it. Let the agent propose while a separate control layer decides whether the action runs. Add circuit breakers and budgets. Keep humans in the loop for anything high impact or irreversible.

I’d sign up to all of it. Now run our Tuesday incident through those controls. The control layer pauses the agent and asks a human to approve. Good. Which human? The CISO can approve containment. That approval settles nothing about the stopped payments, the missed customer deadlines or the regulator’s questions.

Three things are easy to blur here. Identity tells you which agent acted. Permission tells you what it could technically do. Authority tells you whether it was entitled to act, here and now, with these consequences. Identity and access tools handle the first two well. The third lives in the organization, and that’s where the CIO, CISO and CRO stop agreeing.

A permitted action and an authorized decision are different animals.

Three roads, one junction

You know the parable of the blind men and the elephant. AI governance works the same way, except the men are well paid and the elephant now moves on its own.

Each executive has a real problem that looks fine up close. The CIO’s choices make sense where they’re made. One team picks a platform. Another buys an agent. A third builds its own. Together, they create duplicate capabilities, hidden running costs and dependencies that are hard to reverse. The CISO’s controls can pass locally while nobody can say what exposure the business is left carrying. The CRO watches each function rate its own slice of risk, and nobody adds them up.

Map each role’s reasoning end to end, and a pattern emerges. The CIO starts with strategy and investment. The CISO starts with a critical service and its threats. The CRO starts with principal risks. Then all three converge on the same four questions. What’s left over? Is it inside appetite? Who can accept it? When do we look again?

That junction is where ownership goes missing. Agents now reach it in milliseconds.

Plenty of CISOs report to the CIO, and many firms have no CRO. Swap the titles. The functions still need a voice.

Where ownership breaks

The seams fall into three moments: before the agent acts, while it acts and after.

Before, the problem is conflicting authority. Picture a group CISO authorising containment. A subsidiary CEO objects because it would stop a critical service. The incident commander faces a deadline. The agent waits for instructions. Who prevails? If nobody settled that in advance, the loudest voice wins, or the clock does.

During, three things break at once. The person who can order protective action is rarely the one who should accept the cost. The CISO can own the call to isolate a service without owning the stopped payments. Then there’s latency. An approval process that takes forty minutes is useless when the window is five. A slow decision in that window is a governance failure dressed up as diligence. And the governance machinery often fails with the incident. Suppose the identity provider, the approval workflow and the chat tool all sit on the platform that’s down. Your carefully designed authority chain is now out of reach.

Afterward, recovery splits three ways. The CIO says the platform is available. The CISO says it isn’t trusted. The CRO says the leftover exposure might still be too high. All three are right, and the verdicts rarely align. Then comes drift. Models change, suppliers get bought and threats move. James Carse separated finite games, played to win, from infinite games, played to keep the game going. AI approvals are the second kind. You keep them alive, or they quietly go stale.

The fixes everyone reaches for

Everyone reaches for a tidy fix. I’ve proposed a few myself.

Appoint a Chief AI Officer, and one person holds the decision without the three lenses. Form an AI committee, and accountability spreads so thin nobody can find it. Make the CRO the owner, and you lose your independent challenger. Fold the CISO under the CIO, and the board hears nothing but agreement. Buy an agent security platform, and you’ve solved control while leaving authority open.

Each fix answers “Who’s in charge of AI?” The harder question stays put. Who owns this decision, right now?

Own the decision, then own the chain

Split the incident into decisions and give each one an owner. Someone authorizes protective action. Someone accepts the business consequence. Someone accepts the residual risk. Someone authorizes restart. Someone decides whether the original approval still stands. Five people, perhaps, each named before Tuesday arrives.

Give the agent the same treatment. Write its mandate the way you’d brief a new deputy: what it’s for, which decisions it may take, the limits on cost and consequence, when it must escalate and what revokes its authority. Then make that mandate executable, so the control layer checks authority as well as access before anything runs.

Agree the tie-breaks and deputies while everyone’s calm. Set a decision window for each class of decision and test whether your approvals fit inside it. Keep a way to decide when the main systems are down, with narrow, time-limited emergency authority that you reconcile afterwards.

Then capture a decision trail, which goes further than an audit trail. An audit trail says the agent acted at 09:24 and the command succeeded. A decision trail says what evidence existed at 09:24, which authority applied, what consequences were expected, who accepted the remaining risk and what would force a rethink. Build it as decisions happen. Six months later, you shouldn’t depend on interviewing whoever was in the room.

Finally, name one executive who answers for how the decisions fit together. Regulators expect a named person at the end of the line, from the UK’s senior managers regime to DORA, NIS2 and the EU AI Act’s human oversight duties.

What the board should see

Under the UK Corporate Governance Code, directors oversee strategy, risk appetite, principal and emerging risks and material controls. Technology, cyber and AI reporting still tends to reach them as control scores. They need five answers on one page. What changed since we last looked? What now sits outside appetite? Which consequential decisions matter, and who owns them? What evidence supports management’s position? What should trigger renewed challenge?

For agentic AI, add one sharper test. Pick a real autonomous action and ask who authorized it, what justified it, what constrained it, who accepted the consequences and what would make you reconsider it. Crisp answers? Buy everyone lunch. A string of follow-up meetings? You’ve found your work.

Back to Tuesday

Who owned the decision at 09:24? Nobody, in any sense a regulator would accept. The agent had permission. It never had authority, because nobody had defined it.

The fix costs each executive less than it sounds. The CIO keeps architecture. The CISO keeps control strategy. The CRO keeps independent challenge. Each gives up the idea that their slice of the chain is the whole decision.

Agentic AI leaves human accountability in place. It removes the time organizations once had to exercise it.

AI has changed the enterprise architecture. Now we need to change the architecture of the decision.

item.title: Cloud repatriation is on the rise — but tricky questions remain
item.description:
Enterprises are moving to the cloud faster than they have in years. Nearly three-quarters (74%) of IT decision-makers say their organizations sped up cloud migration over the past 12 months, according to Foundry’s 2026 Cloud Computing Study.

Yet a growing number are also bringing some workloads back in-house. About two-thirds (66%) say their organizations have moved or plan to move workloads out of public cloud.

“Repatriation is one part of a wider rethink of where workloads belong,” says Mukesh Ranjan, vice president at Everest Group, a research and advisory firm.

AI workloads are part of the calculus. They’re leaving public cloud nearly as often as storage and databases, and just 13% of IT decision-makers plan to run AI primarily there, according to Foundry’s research. For CIOs, that means deciding workload by workload where each one belongs, with AI adding new factors to weigh, from GPU costs to where models run and where prompts are processed.

Foundry

Selective moves

Foundry’s numbers don’t suggest a mass exodus, however. On average, organizations have moved 22% of their workloads back from public cloud and plan to move another 24% in the next 12 months. One-third of organizations have moved at least a quarter of their workloads back on-premises, down from 37% in 2024.

Many organizations moving workloads out of public cloud may be pulling back only two or three, Ranjan says. They’re certainly not rejecting the public cloud outright.

For global consulting firm Protiviti’s clients, “cloud first” remains the default, says Randy Armknecht, managing director there. “Repatriation is still the exception, driven by a thorough analysis of business value and technical capability,” he says.

Where AI fits in

Security concerns top the reasons organizations give for moving workloads out of public cloud (60%), followed by cost and performance (42% each) and sovereignty (40%), according to the Foundry survey. “Outside manufacturing, AI is a passenger on the repatriation trend driven by cost and security, not driving it directly,” says Armknecht of Protiviti. Ranjan of Everest Group sees AI driving some repatriation, but not most of it.

Even so, AI workloads are among those most often homeward bound. Foundry found that 34% of organizations have already moved AI or ML workloads out of public cloud and another 38% plan to.

Many of those workloads are business systems with AI built in. “Roughly half of what I’ve seen has ‘an AI component,’ and very few are pure ‘AI systems,’” Armknecht says.

Manufacturing is the exception. Many of Protiviti’s industrial clients have embraced AI at the edge to improve efficiency and reduce error rates, Armknecht says, and several tested their models in the cloud before moving them onto local hardware.

Sovereignty concerns have intensified over the past year, especially in Europe. “A year ago, sovereignty was still often discussed as data residency or a compliance checkbox. Today, particularly in Germany and the EU, customers are asking much broader questions: who operates the service, where the dependencies sit, which law applies, and whether critical processes can continue if a major service is unavailable,” says Uwe Geuss, CTO of Retarus, a German provider of enterprise communications services.

AI adds another layer to those questions. “AI makes the sovereignty question more important because it introduces another layer of dependency: not just where data is stored, but where models run, who operates the inference environment, where prompts and documents are processed, and whether sensitive data is being sent into an external AI platform,” Geuss says.

Data control comes first at Framestore, a visual effects and creative studio, followed closely by cost, says Lincoln Wallen, its CTO. The studio builds its own models and fine-tunes open-weight ones, running them on its own infrastructure or through infrastructure-as-a-service providers and tapping major cloud providers for extra capacity. That way, it can adopt new models without rebuilding its systems each time.

Foundry

Sizing up the costs

Whether owning infrastructure costs less than renting it depends largely on how steadily a workload runs. High-volume inference can favor private infrastructure when utilization is high, whereas intermittent demand can make public cloud the better deal, says Ranjan of Everest Group.

“Predictable usage is what makes local hardware pay off, and the need for predictability in spend is another driver for local versus cloud-based AI,” says Armknecht of Protiviti.

Mistakes can prove more expensive on-premises, too. “In the cloud, a sizing mistake costs you a month; on-prem, you live with it for the depreciation cycle,” he adds.

Paying an outside AI service for every interaction can also cost more than running models in-house, Framestore’s Wallen adds. But “public cloud still has an important role,” he says, “especially when businesses need additional capacity or access to specialized capabilities.”

Also at play: cloud savings that didn’t materialize. Idle resources, hard-to-calculate exit fees, and applications lifted and shifted without being adapted to cloud-native capabilities can all erode the expected savings, says Retarus’ Geuss.

“Selective correction of earlier cloud decisions” are among the drivers of repatriation, Ranjan of Everest Group says.

Foundry

Where the pull is strongest

Repatriation makes the most sense where sensitive data, predictable demand, and scale converge, Ranjan says, pointing to banking, healthcare, government, and some industrial workloads as likely candidates. Larger enterprises can more easily absorb the cost of dedicated infrastructure, he adds, though smaller organizations may reach similar outcomes through managed private cloud.

What pushes a company to move workloads varies by industry. Among Protiviti’s clients, defense contractors focus on keeping data on hardware they control, whereas manufacturers want fewer points of failure, which means cutting third-party connections, Armknecht says.

The model question

Many of the most capable AI models are available only as cloud services, because their makers don’t release them to run elsewhere. Open-weight models that are closing in on frontier models are what make AI repatriation practical, according to Armknecht. Framestore, for one, already fine-tunes open-weight models on its own infrastructure.

Fast-improving models can also undercut the case for owning the stack. Tricentis, a software testing company, runs its generative AI workloads on major cloud platforms and keeps only small classification models, such as vision models, on its own hardware.

“Maintaining this infrastructure in production only makes sense for small LLMs that you can assign specific tasks,” says David Colwell, vice president of AI and machine learning at Tricentis. GPUs are scarce and expensive, he says, and at the current pace of improvement, the next general-purpose model from an AI provider would quickly outperform any model Tricentis customized itself. The company keeps its datasets current so it can revisit that choice if base model progress levels off.

Trust is also a factor in which providers Tricentis buys AI from. The company goes through the large cloud providers instead of the AI labs directly, because the cloud providers have long track records protecting Tricentis’s data. “The frontier AI labs are still building that reputation,” Colwell says.

What comes next

Don’t expect a stampede off the public cloud. Protiviti’s Armknecht expects repatriation to continue “at a measured and business-value-driven pace, not a rush or hot trend.”

Workload placement decisions are likely to grow more deliberate across public, private, sovereign, and edge environments, according to Ranjan of Everest Group, with some AI workloads moving back and others starting outside public cloud altogether. “The challenge for CIOs will be maintaining consistent governance and economics across that estate,” he says.

“Many of today’s AI services are excellent at demonstrating what’s possible, but the cost of relying on them for every task could become difficult to sustain as adoption grows,” he says.

CIOs should plan for the day AI is part of nearly every business process, Framestore’s Wallen says, and weigh what it will cost to keep paying outside providers for it. “Many of today’s AI services are excellent at demonstrating what’s possible, but the cost of relying on them for every task could become difficult to sustain as adoption grows,” he says.

IT leaders considering repatriation should check out Networkworld’s deeper look at the challenges and choices: “You’ve decided to repatriate cloud workloads. Now what?”

item.title: What Microsoft’s outage reveals about the economics of prevention
item.description:
Some of the most valuable components of a business process are the ones that appear to accomplish very little. A backup server sits idle. A validation step slows deployment. A rollback capability requires continuing investment even when nobody uses it. To an efficiency-minded executive, these can look like expenditures awaiting a sufficiently enthusiastic cost-reduction initiative.

Of course, their economic contribution becomes considerably less obscure when everything else stops working.

Microsoft’s massive November 12–13 outage offers an instructive example. What began as a disruption involving Exchange Online spread into other parts of the Microsoft 365 ecosystem, interfering with Outlook, Teams, Copilot, SharePoint-related functions and other services on which hundreds of millions of people and countless business processes depend.

According to CIO.com’s reporting, Microsoft found that a large number of servers had become unexpectedly unavailable, overburdening the remaining infrastructure. A process responsible for establishing secure connections became overwhelmed, while some servers returning to service became unresponsive again once traffic resumed. Engineers investigated configuration changes, redistributed traffic, added capacity and worked to restore stability.

The definitive root-cause analysis was still forthcoming as this article was being written. Consequently, it would be premature to conclude that Microsoft failed to invest sufficiently in redundancy, testing or recovery. Nonetheless, the reported sequence provides a useful case for examining how organizations evaluate the economics of processes that prevent failures—or fail to contain them.

And there is a substantial difference between knowing what it costs to keep a system running and understanding the economic consequences when it doesn’t.

The price of a failure is seldom confined to the organization that caused it

The direct financial consequences to Microsoft could include customer service credits, remediation costs, contractual disputes, legal expenses and eventual reputational damage. But those represent only part of the economic picture.

Banks and trading firms experienced communication disruptions. Shipping companies struggled with coordination. Airlines and government agencies encountered interruptions in routine work. According to Reuters, some organizations resorted to telephones, fax machines and other alternatives. Evidently, the digital transformation revolution has not entirely retired the twentieth century.

Cyber-risk modeling firm Kovrr offered a preliminary estimate of approximately $16 billion in lost productivity worldwide, with potential insured losses around $700 million. The firm characterized these figures as rough estimates dependent on assumptions about the outage’s duration and impact. They’re hardly audited damages, and productivity lost temporarily isn’t necessarily economic output lost permanently.

Nevertheless, given the magnitude, this deserves attention. Even if the ultimate damage proves to be a fraction of such estimates, an infrastructure problem originating inside one technology provider can impose consequences that extend far beyond its own financial statements

This is an example of an economic externality: costs imposed on parties other than the organization making the underlying investment and operating decisions.

A cloud provider can calculate its infrastructure costs precisely. It may have far less visibility into the financial consequences of an outage at a hospital, an airline, a pharmaceutical company or a government agency dependent on its services. And contractual limitations on liability may mean that its financial exposure is substantially smaller than the economic damage experienced by customers.

Such asymmetry can distort how much an organization considers it worthwhile to spend on resilience.

The economic contribution of what doesn’t happen

In my earlier CIO.com articles, Business transformation needs a true economic approach, not guesswork and Economic process modeling: Business cases beyond cost accounting, I introduced Economic Process Modeling (EPM) as a way to analyze what business processes actually contribute economically, rather than concentrating primarily on their costs and efficiency.

EPM decomposes a process into four component types (information, actions, systems and people) and examines their economic contribution across five dimensions: revenue, cost and friction, risk, option value and information value.

These dimensions are particularly germane to operational resilience because some activities contribute their greatest economic value by preventing undesirable outcomes.

Consider a redundant server that adds $100,000 annually to infrastructure expense. Its direct cost is readily apparent. But suppose it reduces the annual probability of a $10 million business interruption from 2% to 0.5%. The expected annual loss falls from $200,000 to $50,000. That $150,000 reduction in expected risk exposure exceeds the server’s operating expense, yielding a $50,000 net annual economic benefit.

These are illustrative figures, not estimates of Microsoft’s situation. Their significance lies in the calculation, which is straightforward enough for a spreadsheet–or better yet, an EPM-capable modeling tool. The harder part is recognizing that an apparently underutilized resource deserves to have its risk-mitigation contribution measured in the first place.

An ostensibly idle server may therefore be performing some of the most economically valuable work in the organization. Much like a fire extinguisher, its utilization rate is a rather poor indicator of its worth.

Putting the economics into the process

Microsoft’s outage suggests several places where an EPM analysis could inform resilience decisions, both for technology providers and the enterprises dependent on them.

Table: Applying EPM’s economic lenses to infrastructure resilience. These are prospective analytical applications, not findings that Microsoft lacked the safeguards described.

A distinguishing feature of EPM is that it can account for economic contributions traditional operating metrics and traditional process modeling may overlook.

Take capacity management. A conventional dashboard might show that a server pool is operating at 80% utilization, suggesting an opportunity to consolidate resources. But what happens when a configuration problem removes a quarter of the available capacity? The surviving servers would be asked to handle more work than they can sustain, potentially producing further failures, retries and escalating demand.

The relevant economic question concerns how much risk exposure that reserve capacity mitigates and whether its cost is justified.

Likewise, a rollback process that is rarely invoked may preserve considerable option value—the ability to pursue changes more confidently because a viable recovery path exists. Diagnostic telemetry may have information value far beyond its storage cost if it helps engineers identify the relationship between an infrastructure change, failing health checks and subsequent overload before the problem metastasizes.

Reliability engineers already understand capacity planning, fault isolation, redundancy and rollback. EPM doesn’t supplant these established disciplines. It provides an economic basis for comparing their contributions, allocating investment and deciding which safeguards deserve protection when budgets tighten.

From process maps to economic shock absorbers

In another recent CIO.com article, The next digital twin isn’t of a machine, it’s of your business, I discussed enriching organizational digital twins with the economics of the activities, information, systems and people they represent.

Operational resilience offers a particularly interesting application of this idea.

Imagine modeling an enterprise’s order-to-cash process, including the cloud services on which it depends. A disruption to email might initially appear to be a communications inconvenience. Yet follow the dependencies and the implications become more consequential: customer orders awaiting confirmation, contracts requiring authorization, invoices delayed, shipments held or exceptions going unresolved because the responsible people cannot coordinate.

A traditional process map can show these dependencies. Process mining and observability tools can reveal where the work stops. Risk analysis can identify potential failure scenarios. Economic Process Modeling connects these findings to their economic consequences, allowing leaders to compare the value of alternative safeguards and contingency arrangements.

The analysis may reveal that keeping a modest secondary communication capability available for a few high-value processes is more worthwhile than providing expensive redundant technology to every employee. Or that a manual workaround, seemingly anachronistic during ordinary operations, preserves substantial value during an outage.

Conversely, it might show that certain redundancies cost considerably more than the risk they mitigate.

The objective is economic discipline and discrimination, rather than redundancy for redundancy’s sake.

A more advanced economic digital twin could simulate infrastructure degradation, trace its consequences through dependent processes and estimate the value of alternative interventions before they are deployed. This remains an ambitious application rather than a capability every EPM implementation already possesses, but the underlying logic is well within reach.

Reputation, litigation and the long tail of an outage

A further complication is that the immediate interruption may be only the beginning of the financial consequences.

Enterprise customers seldom abandon a major technology platform overnight, particularly when email, identity, collaboration, security and increasingly AI capabilities are entwined within the same ecosystem. Switching costs can be formidable.

However, an outage can change future purchasing behavior without causing an immediate cancellation. Customers may demand pricing concessions, require stronger contractual protections, defer new deployments or diversify future technology investments. A provider could therefore experience diminished customer lifetime value long after service has been restored.

There may also be legal and regulatory consequences, although the likelihood and magnitude depend on contractual terms, liability limitations and jurisdiction. Customer compensation and insurance recoveries further complicate matters because they transfer financial losses among parties rather than necessarily adding to total economic damage.

An effective EPM assessment would separate the provider’s expected losses from those borne by customers, insurers and others, while avoiding the double counting that can make an impressive estimate rather less impressive under scrutiny.

For CIOs, the larger lesson is that a technology component’s economic significance (even when a seemingly small part of the overall process) should be assessed through the business activities it enables both immediately and downstream, and continuously or periodically. An obscure infrastructure dependency may have an unremarkable operating budget and an extraordinary amount of downstream value at risk.

EPM brings to light that the price tag on the component is a particularly unreliable proxy for the value riding on it.

A little prevention, economically justified

Fortunately, organizations needn’t build a comprehensive digital twin, acquire expensive modeling platforms or assemble a platoon of consultants to begin applying EPM to operational resilience.

Start with one consequential business process and identify the systems, people, decisions and information on which it depends. Examine the credible failure scenarios and estimate their economic consequences, using historical incidents where available and reasonable ranges where evidence is thin. Then evaluate the cost and likely effectiveness of safeguards, workarounds and alternative arrangements.

A workshop involving business, technology, risk and finance leaders, supported by an ordinary process diagram and spreadsheet, can provide an initial economic model. More sophisticated modeling tools become useful as the analysis expands, but sophistication should follow the decision rather than precede it.

The first exercise may reveal an expensive redundancy that adds little protection. It might also reveal that a validation step, an alternate communication channel, a reserve server or a few additional diagnostic signals protect economic value orders of magnitude greater than their costs.

Importantly, EPM cannot anticipate every software defect or guarantee an organization will escape the next outage. It can, however, help reveal where failures are likely to have the greatest financial consequences, which components mitigate those consequences, and which inexpensive interventions deserve priority.

Microsoft’s experience offers a timely reminder that modern business processes are deeply interconnected, and that a technical failure can reverberate through a surprisingly large portion of the economy. The difficulty lies partly in the fact that organizations are much better at accounting for the cost of prevention than for the economic value it preserves.

Perhaps it is time to give the latter a proper place in the business case.

For CIOs and business leaders, applying even a modest amount of Economic Process Modeling could make potentially devastating failures more foreseeable, their consequences more containable and the investments needed to avert them far easier to justify. In many cases, the analysis itself can be done quite inexpensively.

After all, the cheapest outage to recover from is the one that never happens.

item.title: The illusion of AI productivity in software development and what to measure instead
item.description:
Accenture reports that 82% of C-suite leaders are increasing AI investments, signaling continued confidence in the technology. But if you talk to tech leaders, the returns aren’t so clear-cut. AI can write code in seconds, but that’s only the first stage of software development. When AI-generated output introduces errors, misses internal requirements or requires extensive rework, the time saved upfront can quickly disappear.

A report from Bain & Co validates this — AI coding tools are helping developers complete roughly 21% more tasks, but time spent reviewing outputs rose 91%. As engineers generate more code, senior developers face growing review queues. AI can also produce lengthy specifications and documentation that take time to evaluate. This obscures the impact AI adoption is having on the software development lifecycle and, much of the time, simply creates more work.

To understand whether AI is improving productivity, CIOs need to look at the entire process, from the initial idea to software in production.

Building quality controls

At Pearl, we’ve experienced similar aforementioned challenges when using AI to automate parts of our software development process. For example, we asked AI to help create pipeline automation, but it generated GitHub Actions workflows for an engineering environment that uses Azure DevOps and Jenkins. Our astute engineers caught the mismatch during review and had to rewrite the integration.

The code was plausible, but it didn’t account for our actual infrastructure. This is a clear example of how AI-generated code can be convincing despite lacking important context. To catch these instances before advancing too far in the development process, we have a quality-control process that combines AI-assisted review with human oversight based on risk. Lower-risk changes, such as unit tests, can often be reviewed primarily by AI, while critical production-facing code still receives human review. Our AI reviews identify an average of 16 errors per 10 pull requests, including security and architectural issues. The goal is not to remove humans from the review process, but to use automation to catch issues efficiently and reserve human judgment for decisions where risk and complexity warrant it.

Measuring productivity across the entire development lifecycle

Once appropriate quality controls are in place, CIOs need to assess whether AI is delivering measurable productivity gains. AI adoption metrics (token usage, developer participation, etc.) show how much a company is using AI, but not necessarily whether it is becoming more productive. A more useful approach is to track a combination of delivery, effort and quality measures:

  • Engineering cycle time: How long it takes to complete a coding task and get the resulting change into production.
  • End-to-end lead time: How long it takes to move from an initial idea to deployment. This captures delays beyond coding, including review, testing and release.
  • Review and rework time: How much time engineers spend reviewing, debugging and rewriting AI-generated code.
  • Software quality: Defects, security issues and other indicators of reliability. Faster delivery is moot if it creates more problems for teams or customers.

These measures are most useful when considered holistically. Shorter cycle times are encouraging, but leaders should assess whether quality is consistent or improving and whether review and rework are consuming too much time for engineers. Establishing a baseline before expanding AI use, then tracking these measures over time, can help CIOs distinguish genuine improvements from shifts in where work happens.

At Pearl, we track engineering cycle time and have seen it decline month over month in 2026 as our use of AI-generated code has increased. In September 2026, the average pull request we released to production was 75% AI-generated, and 45% of all pull requests were written entirely by AI, with no line edited by a person before commit. These metrics help us assess whether greater AI adoption is translating into faster software delivery, rather than relying on code volume alone.

Rethink workflows

Having a process for assessing AI’s overall impact on productivity helps leadership determine how to allocate employee time. Savvy organizations have taken advantage of AI to automate repetitive tasks so that engineers can focus more on architecture, complex problem-solving and validating results.

As enterprises introduce AI agents that can execute multistep tasks and work together, leaders will also need to rethink how they assign, supervise and evaluate that work. These systems create opportunities to streamline complex workflows, but they also require clear permissions, defined responsibilities and appropriate oversight. Of critical importance is determining where human judgment remains essential and how teams should adapt as more work becomes automated.

For CIOs, the priority should be to redesign engineering workflows around the capabilities of AI, rather than simply adding AI tools to existing processes. This starts with establishing a baseline for development speed and software quality, then measuring how both change as AI adoption increases. It also means using the results to adjust workflows, review requirements and the allocation of engineering time

Ultimately, AI investments should be held accountable to the same business outcomes as any other technology investment. More code, more tokens and broader adoption can indicate progress, but they can be misleading. The real measure of AI productivity is whether an organization can deliver better software faster, with quality and security intact.
